scenes.kicker: F01 · Introduction to Financial Accounting · Module 3
scenes.head: Adjusting entries
scenes.sub: Some changes arrive without a transaction: insurance expires, wages build up, equipment wears. Learn to find, calculate and record the five kinds of month-end adjustment, and to prepare the adjusted trial balance that the financial statements are built from.

segs.say: Adjusting entries. Some changes arrive without a transaction: insurance expires, wages build up, equipment wears. Learn to find, calculate and record the five kinds of month-end adjustment, and to prepare the adjusted trial balance that the financial statements are built from.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Explain why adjusting entries are needed at the end of each period and why they never involve Cash.
Record adjusting entries for prepaid expenses, unearned revenue, accrued revenue, accrued expenses and depreciation.
Calculate straight-line depreciation, accumulated depreciation and book value, including for part of a year.
Calculate accrued interest with I = P × r × t.
Prepare an adjusted trial balance from an unadjusted trial balance and the adjusting entries.
Analyse the effect of omitting an adjustment on net income, assets, liabilities and equity.

scenes.head: At the close of business on 31 March, Lantern’s trial balance balances at $46,860.

segs.say: At the close of business on 31 March, Lantern’s trial balance balances at $46,860. Every transaction of the month has been journalised and posted, yet several balances are out of date. Prepaid Insurance still shows the full $1,800 although a month of cover has gone. Supplies shows $1,500, but a count finds $600 on the shelves. Unearned Revenue still holds all of Harbor Tech’s $2,400 although the first event was catered on 26 March. And nothing records the wages the baristas earned in the second half of March, the interest building up on the bank loan, a month’s wear on the espresso machine, or the breakfast Lantern catered for Pier Nine Studio that morning.

scenes.head: None of these changes came with a transaction.

segs.say: None of these changes came with a transaction. Ledger accounts change only when an entry is posted, and entries are prompted by source documents: invoices, receipts, bank records. Time passing and assets being used up produce no document. An adjusting entry is a journal entry made at the end of a period to bring account balances up to date, so that revenue and expenses fall in the period to which they belong (the accrual basis of lesson 8) and the balance sheet shows the assets and liabilities that actually exist at the period end. Because Lantern reports monthly for this course, it adjusts every month; a business that reports yearly adjusts at least once a year.

scenes.head: Every adjustment falls into one of the four cells of the timing map from lesson 8, or spreads the cost of a long-lived asset as depreciation.

segs.say: Every adjustment falls into one of the four cells of the timing map from lesson 8, or spreads the cost of a long-lived asset as depreciation. Many textbooks, OpenStax among them, count four kinds and treat depreciation as a kind of prepaid expense, because the cost was paid or owed in advance; this course lists it separately because its entry credits a contra account. The table shows each kind, what is wrong before the adjustment, the shape of the entry and Lantern’s examples, numbered a1 to a7.
The five kinds of adjusting entry, with Lantern’s adjustments at 31 March (fictional)

scenes.head: Two features are common to every row.

segs.say: Two features are common to every row. Each adjustment changes at least one income statement account (a revenue or an expense) and at least one balance sheet account (an asset, a contra-asset or a liability). And none of them touches Cash.

scenes.head: Why Cash is never in an adjusting entry

segs.say: Why Cash is never in an adjusting entry. Cash is kept up to date by transactions: every receipt and payment is recorded when it happens, and the bank statement confirms the balance. An adjustment exists because cash and recognition fall in different periods. For a deferral the cash side was recorded earlier, when Lantern paid for the insurance or received the deposit; for an accrual it will be recorded later, when the wages are paid or the customer pays. The adjustment records only the other half, the recognition. If you find yourself writing Cash into an adjusting entry, you are recording a transaction, not an adjustment.

scenes.head: To find the adjustments, accountants walk through the trial balance asking two questions of each account.

segs.say: To find the adjustments, accountants walk through the trial balance asking two questions of each account. Has part of this balance been used up or earned since it was recorded? That question finds the deferrals: Prepaid Insurance, Supplies, Unearned Revenue, Equipment. Has anything been earned or incurred that isn’t recorded at all? That question finds the accruals, which have no balance to prompt you, so they come from checklists, contracts, timesheets and loan agreements: the wages owed, the interest building up, the breakfast not yet invoiced.

scenes.head: A prepaid expense is a cost paid in advance for benefits the business will receive in later periods; until then it is an asset.

segs.say: A prepaid expense is a cost paid in advance for benefits the business will receive in later periods; until then it is an asset. Lantern’s policy cost $1,800 for 12 months from 1 March. By 31 March one month has expired, so 1,800 ÷ 12 = 150 becomes insurance expense (a1). The other $1,650 is still an asset: cover Lantern will receive from April 2026 to February 2027.

scenes.head: Supplies work the same way but are measured by counting.

segs.say: Supplies work the same way but are measured by counting. Lantern doesn’t record each cup and bag of beans as it is used; that would cost more than the information is worth. Instead it counts what is left at the end of the month and works out what must have been used: supplies used = supplies at the start + purchases − supplies on hand, here 0 + 1,500 − 600 = 900 (a2). After the adjustment the Supplies account shows $600, the amount actually on the shelves.
Lantern’s prepaid-expense adjustments (fictional)

scenes.head: Depreciation is the allocation of the cost of a long-lived asset, less its residual value, over its useful life.

segs.say: Depreciation is the allocation of the cost of a long-lived asset, less its residual value, over its useful life. The residual value is what the business expects to get for the asset at the end of the time it plans to use it; the useful life is how long it expects to use it. Depreciation applies the expense recognition principle: the machine helps earn revenue for years, so each period bears part of its cost. It is not an attempt to measure what the asset is worth today.

scenes.head: The straight-line method charges the same amount every period: cost minus residual value, divided by useful life.

segs.say: The straight-line method charges the same amount every period: cost minus residual value, divided by useful life. Lantern’s $12,000 of equipment is expected to last five years with no residual value, so depreciation is (12,000 − 0) ÷ 5 = 2,400 a year, or 2,400 ÷ 12 = 200 a month (a3). Lantern’s policy takes a full month in the month of purchase, so March bears the whole $200 although the machine arrived on 3 March.

scenes.head: The credit doesn’t go to Equipment.

segs.say: The credit doesn’t go to Equipment. It goes to Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment, a contra account with a credit balance that collects all the depreciation recorded so far: its total is the asset’s accumulated depreciation. Equipment keeps showing the original cost of $12,000, and the two together give the book value (called the carrying amount under IFRS): 12,000 − 200 = 11,800 at 31 March. After 12 months accumulated depreciation will be $2,400 and book value $9,600. After 60 months, at the end of February 2031, the machine will be fully depreciated, with a book value of zero, its expected residual value. Keeping cost and accumulated depreciation apart shows a reader both how much was invested and roughly how much of the asset’s life has been used.
Lantern’s depreciation adjustment (fictional)

scenes.head: Part-period conventions

segs.say: Part-period conventions. Lantern’s policy of a full month in the month of purchase is one convention among several. Others charge a full month only for assets bought in the first half of a month, count the exact number of days, or charge half a year in the year of purchase whatever the date. Counting days, Lantern’s machine, bought on 3 March, was in service for 29 of March’s 31 days, giving 200 × 29 ÷ 31 ≈ 187.10. No convention is more correct than another: a business chooses one, applies it consistently, and the total depreciation over the asset’s life is the same.

scenes.head: Harbor Tech paid $2,400 on 8 March for three events, and Lantern recorded the deposit as Unearned Revenue, a liability.

segs.say: Harbor Tech paid $2,400 on 8 March for three events, and Lantern recorded the deposit as Unearned Revenue, a liability. In lesson 8 the five-step model showed that $800 was earned on 26 March, when the first event was catered. The adjustment (a4) moves that $800 from the liability to Catering Revenue; the remaining $1,600 stays as a liability until the April events.
Lantern’s unearned-revenue adjustment (fictional)

scenes.head: Another way to record advance payments

segs.say: Another way to record advance payments. Some businesses record a customer’s advance payment straight into a revenue account, or a prepaid cost straight into an expense account, and adjust at the period end for the part not yet earned or used. The adjusting entry then runs the other way (for example, debit the revenue and credit Unearned Revenue for the part not yet earned), but the adjusted balances end up the same. This course records advances in the balance sheet first, as Lantern does.

scenes.head: Accrued revenue is revenue earned in the period but not yet recorded, because no invoice has been sent or no payment is due yet.

segs.say: Accrued revenue is revenue earned in the period but not yet recorded, because no invoice has been sent or no payment is due yet. Lantern catered Pier Nine Studio’s breakfast on 31 March and will send the $600 invoice on 2 April. The performance obligation has been satisfied, so March has earned the revenue, and Lantern has a right to be paid: an account receivable (a7). Sending the invoice in April records nothing new, because the receivable already exists; when Pier Nine pays, Lantern debits Cash and credits Accounts Receivable. Interest earned on money Lantern had lent would be accrued the same way, through Interest Receivable and Interest Revenue.
Lantern’s accrued-revenue adjustment (fictional)

scenes.head: An accrued expense is an expense incurred in the period but not yet paid or recorded.

segs.say: An accrued expense is an expense incurred in the period but not yet paid or recorded. The baristas were paid on 20 March for 1–15 March. By 31 March they have earned another $1,400 for 16–31 March, to be paid on 5 April. March used their work, so March bears the expense; Lantern owes the money, so a liability, Wages Payable, appears (a5). On 5 April Lantern will debit Wages Payable and credit Cash for $1,400: the payment settles the liability and is not a second expense.

scenes.head: Interest builds up day by day on a loan.

segs.say: Interest builds up day by day on a loan. Simple interest for part of a year is I = P × r × t: principal times the annual rate times the time in years. Lantern’s $10,000 note at 6% a year accrues 10,000 × 0.06 × 1/12 = 50 in March (a6). The first payment, due on 1 June, will cover three months: 10,000 × 0.06 × 3/12 = 150. If Lantern accrues $50 at the end of March, April and May, Interest Payable will stand at $150 on 31 May, and the payment on 1 June (debit Interest Payable, credit Cash) clears it without any new expense. Loan agreements may also measure time in days over a 360-day or 365-day year; the contract says which.
Lantern’s accrued-expense adjustments (fictional)

scenes.head: After the seven adjustments are journalised and posted, Lantern lists every account again.

segs.say: After the seven adjustments are journalised and posted, Lantern lists every account again. The adjusted trial balance shows each account’s balance after the adjustments; it checks that debits still equal credits and is the source from which the financial statements are prepared in lesson 10.
Lantern Coffee Co.: adjusted trial balance at 31 March 2026 (fictional)

scenes.head: The total rose from $46,860 to $49,110, by $2,250, although the adjustments add up to $4,100.

segs.say: The total rose from $46,860 to $49,110, by $2,250, although the adjustments add up to $4,100. Three of them only move an amount between two accounts on the same side: a1 and a2 move debit balance from an asset to an expense, and a4 moves credit balance from a liability to a revenue, so they leave the totals unchanged. The other four add a new amount to both sides: 200 + 1,400 + 50 + 600 = 2,250. A balanced adjusted trial balance shows only that each adjustment was recorded with equal debits and credits; it can’t show that an adjustment was forgotten.

scenes.head: An omitted adjustment leaves out both its debit and its credit, so the trial balance still balances and the error has to be found by thinking, not by…

segs.say: An omitted adjustment leaves out both its debit and its credit, so the trial balance still balances and the error has to be found by thinking, not by adding up. Each omission misstates an income statement total and a balance sheet total by the same amount, and until the books are closed, equity is misstated by the same amount as net income.
What each of Lantern’s adjustments would misstate if it were left out (fictional)

scenes.head: Two patterns make the table easy to rebuild.

segs.say: Two patterns make the table easy to rebuild. Leaving out an expense overstates net income and equity; leaving out revenue understates them. Omitted deferral adjustments leave a balance sheet figure too high (an asset not yet used up, a liability not yet earned off), while omitted accruals leave one too low (a receivable or payable that is missing). With all seven left out, Lantern would report net income of $2,290 instead of $990, total assets of $43,150 instead of $42,500, liabilities of $21,160 instead of $21,810 and equity of $21,990 instead of $20,690.

scenes.head: Several adjustments rest on estimates: the machine’s five-year life and nil residual value, the supplies count, the date on which an event counts as…

segs.say: Several adjustments rest on estimates: the machine’s five-year life and nil residual value, the supplies count, the date on which an event counts as delivered. If Ana later expects the machine to last only four years, the depreciation charge changes from then on; later courses show how. Estimates should be reasonable, supported by evidence and applied consistently. They are also where auditors look hardest, because a small change in a useful life or an accrual can move profit without any cash changing hands.

scenes.head: Straight-line depreciation (per year)

segs.say: Straight-line depreciation (per year): Depreciation per year = (Cost − Residual value)/(Useful life).
Cost: What the asset cost to buy and get ready for use ($).
Residual value: What the business expects to get for the asset at the end of its useful life ($).
Useful life: How long the business expects to use the asset (years).
It assumes this: The asset’s benefits are used up evenly over its life.
Other methods (declining balance, units of production) exist; F02 covers them.

scenes.head: Straight-line depreciation for part of a year

segs.say: Straight-line depreciation for part of a year: Depreciation = (Cost − Residual value)/(Useful life) × m/12.
m: Months the asset is in use during the period, counted by the business’s convention (months).
Lantern counts a full month in the month of purchase: 2,400 × 1/12 = 200 for March.

scenes.head: Book value (carrying amount)

segs.say: Book value (carrying amount): Book value = Cost − Accumulated depreciation.
Accumulated depreciation: All depreciation recorded on the asset since it was bought ($).
Book value is an allocation of cost, not a market value.

scenes.head: Simple interest for a period

segs.say: Simple interest for a period: I = P × r × t.
I: Interest for the period ($).
P: Principal: the amount borrowed or lent ($).
r: Annual interest rate, as a decimal (6% = 0.06).
t: Time in years (one month = 1/12) (years).
It assumes this: Interest is not compounded within the period.

scenes.head: Supplies used in a period

segs.say: Supplies used in a period: Supplies used = Supplies at start + Purchases − Supplies on hand.
Supplies at start: Balance of the Supplies account at the start of the period ($).
Purchases: Supplies bought during the period ($).
Supplies on hand: Cost of supplies counted at the end of the period ($).

chapters.title: Example: An online retailer’s rent and packaging

scenes.head: An online retailer’s rent and packaging

segs.say: Parcelwise, a fictional online retailer, paid $2,400 on 1 October for six months’ warehouse rent (October to March) and debited Prepaid Rent. Its Supplies account for packaging showed $300 on 1 October; it bought $1,250 of packaging during the quarter, and a count on 31 December finds $400 left. Its financial year ends on 31 December. Prepare the two adjusting entries.

scenes.head: An online retailer’s rent and packaging

segs.say: Step 1. Rent is a prepaid expense. The cost per month is 2,400 ÷ 6 = 400; October to December is three months, so 3 × 400 = 1,200 has been used.
Step 2. Entry: debit Rent Expense 1,200; credit Prepaid Rent 1,200. Prepaid Rent is left at 2,400 − 1,200 = 1,200, the rent for January to March.
Step 3. Packaging used = start + purchases − on hand: 300 + 1,250 − 400 = 1,150.
Step 4. Entry: debit Supplies Expense 1,150; credit Supplies 1,150. Supplies is left at 400, the amount counted. Neither entry involves Cash: the cash was recorded when Parcelwise paid.

scenes.head: An online retailer’s rent and packaging

segs.say: Debit Rent Expense $1,200, credit Prepaid Rent $1,200; debit Supplies Expense $1,150, credit Supplies $1,150.

Without these entries the quarter’s expenses would be $2,350 too low, profit $2,350 too high, and assets overstated by the same amount: rent already used and packaging already shipped out would still be reported as resources.

chapters.title: Example: A van, its loan and a choice of convention

scenes.head: A van, its loan and a choice of convention

segs.say: Halden Home Energy, a fictional battery-storage installer, buys a van on 1 September 2026 for $43,000, expecting to use it for five years and then sell it for $7,000. It pays $3,000 in cash and the rest with a $40,000 bank loan at 7.5% a year, interest due each 31 August. Halden uses straight-line depreciation with a full month in the month of purchase; its financial year ends on 31 December. Record the adjustments at 31 December 2026, find the van’s book value, state the effect on the year’s results, and say how a half-year convention would change 2026.

scenes.head: A van, its loan and a choice of convention

segs.say: Step 1. Depreciable amount: 43,000 − 7,000 = 36,000. Per year 36,000 ÷ 5 = 7,200; per month 7,200 ÷ 12 = 600.
Step 2. September to December is four months: 4 × 600 = 2,400. Entry: debit Depreciation Expense 2,400; credit Accumulated Depreciation—Van 2,400. Book value 43,000 − 2,400 = 40,600.

Step 3. Interest for four months: 40,000 × 0.075 × 4/12 = 1,000. Entry: debit Interest Expense 1,000; credit Interest Payable 1,000. The payment on 31 August 2027, 40,000 × 0.075 = 3,000, will settle the 1,000 owed for 2026 and 2,000 of 2027’s interest.

Step 4. Effect on 2026: expenses rise by 3,400, so net income and equity fall by 3,400; assets fall by 2,400 (through the contra account) and liabilities rise by 1,000. Check: −2,400 = 1,000 + (−3,400).

Step 5. Under a half-year convention 2026 would bear 7,200 ÷ 2 = 3,600 of depreciation, 1,200 more than under Halden’s policy. Total depreciation over the van’s life is 36,000 either way; only the timing changes.

scenes.head: A van, its loan and a choice of convention

segs.say: Debit Depreciation Expense $2,400, credit Accumulated Depreciation—Van $2,400; debit Interest Expense $1,000, credit Interest Payable $1,000. Book value at 31 December 2026: $40,600. Net income for 2026 falls by $3,400 (by $4,600 under a half-year convention).

Buying the van on credit put a $43,000 asset and a $40,000 liability on the books, but the cost of using them appears only through adjustments: depreciation for the wear and interest for the borrowing. A reader comparing two installers should check which depreciation convention each uses before comparing their first-year profits.

chapters.title: Example: Whose profit pays the bonus?

scenes.head: Whose profit pays the bonus?

segs.say: The general manager of a fictional hotel earns a bonus of 2% of annual net income before the bonus. On 31 December the unadjusted trial balance shows net income of $840,000, and the manager asks to be paid on that figure. The controller has not yet recorded: depreciation of $210,000; staff wages of $36,000 earned in the last week of December; $48,000 of deposits that are now earned because the guests stayed in December; $12,000 of interest accrued on the hotel’s mortgage; and $18,000 of prepaid insurance that has expired. What should the bonus be?

scenes.head: Whose profit pays the bonus?

segs.say: Step 1. Classify each item and its effect on net income: depreciation, an expense (−210,000); accrued wages, an expense (−36,000); deposits earned, revenue (+48,000); accrued interest, an expense (−12,000); expired insurance, an expense (−18,000).
Step 3. Bonus on the adjusted figure: 0.02 × 612,000 = 12,240. On the unadjusted figure it would be 0.02 × 840,000 = 16,800, an overpayment of 16,800 − 12,240 = 4,560.

scenes.head: Whose profit pays the bonus?

segs.say: The bonus should be $12,240, based on adjusted net income of $612,000, not $16,800.

Contracts that depend on profit, such as bonuses, profit shares and loan covenants, should say that profit means the adjusted (and usually audited) figure. Most of the gap here comes from depreciation, an expense no invoice ever prompts, which is exactly why a manager paid on profit has an interest in adjustments being forgotten.

scenes.head: An interactive

segs.say: Work through Lantern’s seven adjustments. For each one choose the accounts, the direction and side of each change, the amount, the effect on the accounting equation and the statements affected. Notice that Cash never appears. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Straight-line depreciation and book value

segs.say: Change the cost, residual value, useful life and the months the asset is used in its first financial year. The default is Lantern’s machine with a full first year. Try 10 months, as for a machine bought in March by a business whose year ends in December, and watch depreciation spread over an extra, partial year. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Accrued interest: I = P × r × t

segs.say: Interest Payable builds up month by month and is cleared by each payment. The default is Lantern’s note: $10,000 at 6%, with interest paid every three months. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: An interactive

segs.say: Post March’s fifteen transactions, then the seven adjustments, and watch the trial balance total move from $46,860 to $49,110. Which adjustments change the total, and which only move an amount within one side? Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “Accrued wages: debit Wages Expense, credit Cash.”

segs.say: “Accrued wages: debit Wages Expense, credit Cash.”. Nothing has been paid on 31 March, so Cash can’t change. The credit goes to a liability, Wages Payable. Cash appears on 5 April, when the payment settles that liability. If an entry contains Cash, it is a transaction, not an adjustment.

scenes.head: “Supplies expense is what the count shows.”

segs.say: “Supplies expense is what the count shows.”. The count is what is left: it becomes the new balance of the Supplies asset. The expense is what was used: start + purchases − count. Lantern counted $600, so it used $1,500 − $600 = $900, not $600.

scenes.head: “Depreciation: credit Equipment.”

segs.say: “Depreciation: credit Equipment.”. Equipment stays at its cost; depreciation is credited to the contra account Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment, so a reader can see both the original cost and how much has been allocated. And depreciation is not a fall in market value: it spreads cost over the years of use.

scenes.head: “A 6% loan of $10,000 costs $600 of interest this month.”

segs.say: “A 6% loan of $10,000 costs $600 of interest this month.”. Interest rates are quoted per year. One month is 1/12 of a year: 10,000 × 0.06 × 1/12 = 50. Always convert the time into years before multiplying.

scenes.head: “When the accrued wages are paid, record Wages Expense again.”

segs.say: “When the accrued wages are paid, record Wages Expense again.”. The expense was recognised on 31 March by the adjustment. On 5 April the payment only settles the liability: debit Wages Payable, credit Cash. Debiting Wages Expense again would count March’s wages twice, once in March and once in April.

scenes.head: “The adjusted trial balance balances, so no adjustment is missing.”

segs.say: “The adjusted trial balance balances, so no adjustment is missing.”. An omitted adjustment leaves out both its debit and its credit, so the totals still agree. Only a systematic review (each balance questioned, a checklist of accruals) finds what is missing.

scenes.head: In a business of any size, adjustments are part of a routine called the month-end close.

segs.say: In a business of any size, adjustments are part of a routine called the month-end close. The accountant works from a checklist of recurring items: prepayments are expensed from a schedule that lists each policy and contract, depreciation comes from a fixed-asset register that records each asset’s cost, life and convention, accrued payroll comes from timesheets, interest from the loan agreements, and unbilled revenue from records of work completed but not invoiced. Many of these entries are prepared in the same way every month, which is why Lantern’s a1, a3 and a6 will recur in April with the same amounts.

scenes.head: The items that are not routine call for judgement, and that is where the risk lies.

segs.say: The items that are not routine call for judgement, and that is where the risk lies. Whether a job was finished on 31 March or 1 April, whether a deposit has been earned, and what useful life to give a new van all move profit between periods without any cash changing hands. Auditors therefore test adjustments with evidence: they look at delivery records near the period end to check that revenue is in the right period, compare accrued wages with the next payroll, and ask whether useful lives match how long similar assets have actually lasted.

scenes.head: Decisions depend on these numbers.

segs.say: Decisions depend on these numbers. The hotel’s bonus in the applied example would have been overpaid by $4,560 on unadjusted figures. Loan covenants work the same way: Coastline Bank tests Lantern’s liabilities against its equity, and on unadjusted figures Lantern would appear to owe $650 less and own $1,300 more equity than it really does. When Ana prices her April events or decides whether to hire, she should use March’s adjusted net income of $990, not the $2,290 her unadjusted trial balance shows.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Adjusting entries bring accounts up to date at the end of a period for changes that come with no transaction: time passing, assets used, revenue earned and costs incurred.
There are five kinds: prepaid expenses and unearned revenue (deferrals), accrued revenue and accrued expenses (accruals), and depreciation.
Every adjustment changes at least one income statement account and one balance sheet account, and never Cash.
Straight-line depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life, credited to accumulated depreciation, a contra-asset; book value = cost − accumulated depreciation.
Interest accrues as I = P × r × t, with r per year and t in years. Supplies used = start + purchases − count.
Lantern’s seven adjustments reduce net income from $2,290 to $990 and raise the trial balance total from $46,860 to $49,110.
A missed adjustment doesn’t unbalance the trial balance; it misstates net income and equity, and one of assets or liabilities, by the same amount.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
